quantitative_questions.question_text: Suppose the federal minimum wage were increased to $15.00 per hour. Approximately what percentage of low-wage workers whose wages would increase because of the policy do you think would become unemployed as a result? Click here to see the source and assumptions that will be used for benchmarking.
quantitative_questions.benchmark_source: Congressional Budget Office (2021), The Budgetary Effects of the Raise the Wage Act of 2021
quantitative_questions.benchmark_assumptions:
How is the correct answer determined?

Your answer to this question will be compared with a benchmark derived from the following published research.

Source: Congressional Budget Office (2021), The Budgetary Effects of the Raise the Wage Act of 2021.

The Congressional Budget Office analyzed a proposal to gradually increase the federal minimum wage to $15.00 per hour.

The Congressional Budget Office projected both the reduction in employment and the number of low-wage workers whose wages would increase because of the policy. The benchmark used in this study is calculated by dividing the projected reduction in employment by the total number of low-wage workers whose wages were projected to increase.
quantitative_questions.notes: Internal derivation: 1.4 million projected reduction in employment divided by 27 million workers projected to receive higher wages = 5.2% of workers becoming unemployed. The denominator is 17 million directly affected workers plus 10 million indirectly affected workers.

claims.claim_text: The current federal minimum wage is too low for a full-time worker to cover basic living expenses.
claims.notes: Audited and upgraded; Davidson County benchmark locked.

facts.fact_text: A nationwide analysis finds that a full-time worker earning the federal minimum wage cannot afford basic necessities anywhere in the United States.
facts.source_name: Drexel University Center for Hunger-Free Communities

facts.fact_text: A nationwide analysis finds that a full-time worker earning the federal minimum wage cannot afford a modest one-bedroom apartment in most areas of the United States.
facts.source_name: National Low Income Housing Coalition, Out of Reach
facts.notes: Housing affordability evidence; replaces older demographic fact.

facts.fact_text: It is difficult to determine whether the federal minimum wage is enough to cover basic living expenses because the income needed depends heavily on factors such as household size, location, government benefits, financial support from family members, and other individual circumstances.
facts.notes: Methodological con fact; challenges generality of living-wage claim.

facts.fact_text: Many minimum-wage workers live in households with multiple earners, so whether they can cover their basic living expenses often depends on their household's combined income rather than on the worker's own wages alone.

quantitative_questions.question_text: Suppose a single adult with no children lives in Davidson County (Nashville), Tennessee, which was selected because its cost of living is similar to that of many U.S. communities. This person works full-time (40 hours per week, 52 weeks per year) earning the current federal minimum wage of $7.25 per hour. Approximately what percentage of this person's annual basic living expenses would be covered by their full-time earnings? Click here to see the source and assumptions that will be used for benchmarking.
quantitative_questions.units_label: % of annual basic living expenses covered
quantitative_questions.benchmark_source: MIT Living Wage Calculator, Davidson County, Tennessee
quantitative_questions.benchmark_assumptions: Single adult, no children; Davidson County, Tennessee; full-time work at 40 hours/week and 52 weeks/year; federal minimum wage $7.25/hour compared to MIT living wage of $24.64/hour.
quantitative_questions.notes: Internal derivation: annual earnings at $7.25/hour for 40 hours/week and 52 weeks/year = $15,080; MIT living wage for Davidson County single adult/no children is $24.64/hour, or $51,251.20 annually; $15,080 / $51,251.20 = 29.4%, rounded to 29%.

A nationwide study following independent businesses after minimum-wage increases found that many firms adapted through changes such as higher prices and improved productivity rather than closing.

policies.proposal_text: The United States should adopt a carbon-pricing policy.
policies.debate_summary: A carbon-pricing policy charges for carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels. Supporters argue that it would reduce greenhouse-gas emissions and slow climate change. Opponents argue that it would increase energy costs and harm some industries or overall economic growth.
policies.notes: Carbon-pricing policy module locked from working-table discussion. Includes five claims.

claims.claim_text: Carbon pricing substantially reduces greenhouse-gas emissions.
claims.notes: Fifth policy-module claim set includes policy effectiveness.

facts.fact_text: A systematic review of 80 evaluations of carbon-pricing policies around the world finds that carbon pricing usually reduces emissions.
A study of 121 countries finds that higher carbon taxes are associated with lower carbon dioxide emissions over time.
facts.source_name: Cross-country panel study of carbon taxes and CO₂ emissions

facts.fact_text: A review of empirical studies concludes that existing carbon-pricing policies have often produced only modest emissions reductions because prices were usually low and coverage was limited.
facts.source_name: Review of empirical ex post evidence on carbon pricing and technological change
facts.notes: Challenges depth/durability of emissions reductions rather than direction.

facts.fact_text: A review of evidence from 19 carbon taxes concludes that the emissions reductions from carbon taxes have generally been small under the carbon prices actually used.
facts.notes: Challenges magnitude under real-world carbon tax levels.

quantitative_questions.question_text: In evaluations of real-world carbon-pricing policies, approximately what percentage reduction in greenhouse-gas emissions does carbon pricing typically produce? Click here to see the source and assumptions that will be used for benchmarking.
quantitative_questions.benchmark_assumptions: Benchmark uses the review's central estimate that real-world carbon-pricing policies typically reduce emissions by about 10%, with estimates varying across policies and study designs.
quantitative_questions.status: Locked; reconstructed from locked source discussion
quantitative_questions.notes: Internal derivation: benchmark is the review's central estimate that real-world carbon-pricing policies typically reduce emissions by about 10%.

claims.claim_text: Greenhouse-gas emissions are causing substantial environmental and economic harm.
claims.notes: Need-for-policy claim; benchmark uses Burke, Hsiang & Miguel global GDP projection.

facts.fact_text: The IPCC concludes that climate change has already caused widespread harm to ecosystems, people, settlements, and infrastructure.
facts.source_name: IPCC AR6 Synthesis Report / Working Group II

facts.fact_text: A global study projects that continued climate change would cause large increases in heat-related mortality, with the greatest impacts occurring in hotter and lower-income regions.
facts.source_name: Carleton et al., Quarterly Journal of Economics

facts.fact_text: A review of research concludes that people, businesses, and governments adapt to changing climate conditions in many ways, reducing many of the projected economic impacts of climate change.

A review of economic studies concludes that estimates of future climate damages vary widely across models because they rely on different assumptions about adaptation, technological change, and how climate change affects economic activity.
facts.source_name: NGFS damage-function review / National Academies damage-function literature

claims.claim_text: Carbon pricing places a substantial financial burden on households by increasing their energy costs.
claims.notes: Household cost claim; benchmark uses Columbia/Rhodium modeling.

facts.fact_text: A review of carbon-pricing policies concludes that businesses typically pass much of the cost of carbon pricing on to consumers through higher prices for gasoline, electricity, and other energy sources.
Studies of British Columbia's carbon tax find that much of the tax was passed on to consumers through higher gasoline prices.
Analyses of proposed carbon-pricing policies conclude that although household energy costs increase, the overall financial impact on most households is generally modest.
facts.notes: Challenges substantiality of household burden; source URL should receive final source-url audit.

facts.fact_text: A review of household impacts concludes that the direct increase in energy costs from many proposed carbon-pricing policies amounts to only a small percentage of household income.
facts.notes: Direct household burden relative to income.

claims.claim_text: Carbon pricing imposes substantial economic costs on firms and workers, especially in carbon-intensive industries such as steel, cement, chemicals, and petroleum refining.
claims.notes: Industry-performance claim revised to use concrete industry examples; benchmark uses composite RFF production measure.

facts.fact_text: A study of carbon-pricing policies finds that carbon-intensive industries experience declines in employment after carbon pricing is introduced.
facts.notes: Employment channel in carbon-intensive industries; source URL should receive final source-url audit.

facts.fact_text: A study of European firms finds that higher carbon prices reduced investment and sales among many carbon-intensive firms.
facts.source_name: ECB working paper on carbon prices and firm investment

facts.fact_text: A review of research concludes that although carbon pricing reduces employment in some carbon-intensive industries, it primarily reallocates workers to other sectors, resulting in relatively small effects on overall employment.
facts.source_name: Resources for the Future employment explainer
facts.notes: Worker reallocation rather than aggregate job destruction.

facts.fact_text: A review of empirical studies concludes that carbon pricing has generally had little effect on the competitiveness of firms in most carbon-intensive industries, and when measurable effects are found, they are usually small.
facts.source_name: OECD review: Carbon Pricing and Competitiveness
facts.notes: Competitiveness of firms in carbon-intensive industries.

claims.claim_text: Carbon pricing substantially reduces long-run economic growth.
claims.notes: Aggregate GDP-growth claim; added after carbon module review.

facts.fact_text: A review of economic models concludes that carbon pricing reduces long-run GDP relative to a world without carbon pricing.

facts.fact_text: A study of the European Union's Emissions Trading System finds that higher carbon prices were associated with lower GDP.
facts.source_name: Empirical analysis of EU ETS macroeconomic effects

facts.fact_text: A study of European carbon taxes finds no evidence that carbon pricing reduced countries' economic growth over the following decade.
A review of economic models concludes that moderate carbon-pricing policies generally have only small effects on long-run economic growth.
facts.source_name: IMF review of carbon-pricing macroeconomic models
facts.notes: Challenges magnitude of modeled GDP effects.
